The Short Version Best overall under $400: Bambu Lab A1 — the closest thing to “it just works” at this price. Best print quality for the money: Elegoo Centauri Carbon — beats machines $200 more expensive. Best dirt-cheap entry: Creality Ender 3 V3 — if your budget is truly tight and you don’t mind tinkering. Best for tiny spaces: Bambu Lab A1 Mini — small footprint, surprisingly capable. If you want one sentence: get the Bambu Lab A1 if you want zero hassle, or the Elegoo Centauri Carbon if print quality matters more than ecosystem polish.
What “Budget” Actually Means in 2026 The budget segment changed. Three years ago, “budget” meant a bed-slinger kit you assembled yourself and tuned for a weekend before getting a decent print. In 2026, sub-$400 machines ship with auto bed leveling, vibration compensation, and slicer profiles that work out of the box. The floor has risen dramatically.
That means the real question isn’t “will it print” — they all print now. It’s “how much of my time will it cost me,” “how good is the output,” and “what’s the ecosystem like when something goes wrong.”
1. Bambu Lab A1 — Best Overall The A1 is what happens when a company optimizes for the new-user experience instead of spec-sheet bragging rights. Auto calibration, fast and quiet operation, and the smoothest software pipeline in the price range. You unbox it, run the calibration, and you’re printing usable parts in under an hour.
Strengths:
Genuinely hands-off. The calibration routine handles flow, vibration, and bed mesh automatically. Excellent first-layer consistency — the thing most beginners struggle with. Quiet enough to run in a bedroom or office. AMS Lite support for multi-color if you want to add it later. Weaknesses:
Bambu’s ecosystem is somewhat walled. You can use third-party filament, but the smoothest path is theirs. Cloud-connected by default (local-only mode exists but is less polished). Who it’s for: Anyone who wants to make things, not tune machines. First-time buyers, gift recipients, and people whose time is worth more than the $50-100 they’d save going cheaper.
Check the Bambu Lab A1 price on Amazon → 2. Elegoo Centauri Carbon — Best Print Quality for the Money We’ve reviewed the Centauri Carbon in depth after 6 months of daily printing. Short version: the print quality punches well above the price. At 0.2mm with tuned settings, surface finish rivals machines costing significantly more.
Strengths:
Best out-of-box print quality in this price tier. Handles a wide filament range — PLA, PETG, TPU, PLA-CF, ABS — once you do a tuning pass per material. Strong value if you care about the final part more than the journey. Weaknesses:
Louder than the Bambu A1. Elegoo’s marketing understates this. Slightly more tuning required per filament type. Who it’s for: People who want the best-looking prints per dollar and don’t mind a tuning pass. Hobbyists who’ll print in a garage or workshop where noise doesn’t matter.
Check the Elegoo Centauri Carbon price on Amazon → 3. Creality Ender 3 V3 — Best Truly Cheap Option The Ender line is the reason desktop 3D printing went mainstream, and the V3 modernizes it with auto-leveling and a faster core. It’s still the budget-budget pick: the lowest entry price that still produces good results.
Strengths:
Lowest price of any printer worth recommending. Massive community — every problem has been solved and documented somewhere. Endlessly upgradeable and moddable. Weaknesses:
More hands-on than the Bambu or Elegoo. You will tinker. Quality control varies unit to unit. Who it’s for: Tight budgets, tinkerers, and people who want to learn how the machine actually works.
Check the Creality Ender 3 V3 price on Amazon → 4. Bambu Lab A1 Mini — Best for Small Spaces Same hands-off philosophy as the A1, shrunk down. The smaller build volume (180mm cubed) is the only real compromise. If you’re printing miniatures, small functional parts, or just don’t have desk space, this is the pick.
Strengths:
Tiny footprint, fits on a crowded desk. Same easy calibration and quiet operation as the full A1. Often the cheapest way into the Bambu ecosystem. Weaknesses:
Small build volume rules out larger prints. Who it’s for: Apartment dwellers, miniature painters, and anyone whose constraint is space, not ambition.
Check the Bambu Lab A1 Mini price on Amazon → How to Choose (Decision Shortcut) You want zero hassle: Bambu Lab A1. You want the best-looking prints per dollar: Elegoo Centauri Carbon. Your budget is genuinely tight: Creality Ender 3 V3. You’re short on space: Bambu Lab A1 Mini. What You’ll Also Need A printer is the start, not the whole cost. Budget for:
Filament — start with PLA . One or two 1kg spools. (See our filament guide.) A scraper or spatula for part removal (usually included, but a good one helps). A small toolkit — hex keys, flush cutters, a deburring tool. Optional but worth it: an enclosure if you’ll print ABS, and a dry box if you live somewhere humid. Bottom Line The budget 3D printer market in 2026 is the best it’s ever been. You genuinely cannot make a bad choice among these four — they all print well. Match the machine to your priority: hassle-free (Bambu A1), print quality (Elegoo Centauri Carbon), lowest price (Ender 3 V3), or smallest footprint (A1 Mini).

content:
I’ve been printing on the Elegoo Centauri Carbon almost every day since late 2025. This isn’t a first-impressions review. This is what happens after hundreds of prints, multiple filament types, and a lot of troubleshooting.
The Short Version The Centauri Carbon is a strong mid-range printer that punches above its price. Print quality is excellent out of the box. Speed is competitive. Noise is the biggest weakness, and Elegoo’s marketing understates how loud it actually is.
If you’re choosing between this and a Bambu Lab A1, the Centauri Carbon wins on print quality and loses on ecosystem (Bambu’s software integration is smoother). If you’re choosing between this and an older Ender 3 variant, there’s no contest. Get the Centauri.
Print Quality This is where the Centauri earns its keep. At 0.2mm layer height with properly tuned settings, surface finish is clean with minimal visible layer lines. Overhangs hold well up to about 55 degrees before you need supports.
I’ve printed with PLA, Rapid PLA+, PETG, Rapid PETG, TPU, PLA-CF, ABS, glow-in-the-dark PLA, and food-grade PETG on this machine. Every filament type required its own tuning pass in OrcaSlicer, but once dialed in, results are consistent print to print.
Best results I’ve gotten:
PLA/PLA+: Nearly flawless at stock speeds. Gyroid infill at 15% for daily-use objects. PETG: Required slower first layer and higher bed temp. Food-grade CARBON PETG at 0.2mm layer height with 0.42-0.5mm line widths worked well after tuning. TPU: Print slow (30mm/s max) with direct drive and disable retraction. Results are good but impatient people will hate this. ABS: Needs the door closed and ambient temp management. I print in a closet with the door shut, which helps. Speed Competitive but not class-leading. Rapid PLA+ at the printer’s recommended “fast” profile gives solid results without visible quality loss. But if you’re coming from a Bambu Lab P1S or X1C expecting similar speeds, calibrate your expectations down slightly.
Where speed matters most: first layers. The Centauri handles first layers cleanly at moderate speeds, which means fewer failed prints and less wasted time overall.
Noise Here’s where I’d push back on Elegoo’s marketing. It’s not quiet. In a closet with foam padding around it and the door closed, it’s still clearly audible from the next room. If you’re planning to run this in a bedroom or shared living space, plan for noise management.
What I’ve done:
Placed the printer on foam pads from the original packaging Closed the closet door during prints Exploring better soundproofing solutions It’s livable, but if noise sensitivity is a priority, factor in $30-50 for proper vibration dampening (concrete paver + foam pad sandwich works better than the stock feet).
Slicer Situation I use OrcaSlicer v2.3.0. Elegoo ships a PrusaSlicer-based slicer that works fine but lacks some of OrcaSlicer’s features (better support painting, pressure advance tuning, more granular speed controls).
One thing that matters: when building filament profiles in OrcaSlicer, use the exact field names from the UI. If you’re following online guides that reference different field names, you’ll waste time hunting for settings that are labeled differently. I’ve built complete profiles for Hatchbox ABS, CARBON FDA PETG, Hatchbox Glow-in-the-Dark PLA, and Polymaker Draft PLA. Happy to share settings if people want them.
Filament Dryer Pairing I use the Polymaker PolyDryer alongside the Centauri Carbon. Considered the Sunlu S2 but the Polymaker has better drying consistency and integrates better with filament storage. If you’re printing PETG or TPU regularly, a dryer isn’t optional. Wet filament on this printer produces stringing and surface defects that no amount of retraction tuning will fix.
Reliability After 6 Months Two issues in hundreds of prints:
One partial clog that cleared with a cold pull Bed adhesion issues that turned out to be a dirty build plate (isopropyl alcohol fixed it permanently) No mechanical failures, no board issues, no firmware bugs that affected prints. The machine just works.
Who Should Buy This Someone stepping up from an entry-level printer (Ender 3, Neptune, etc.) who wants noticeably better quality Someone who wants to print multiple filament types without constant hardware modifications Someone who prioritizes print quality over raw speed Who Should Look Elsewhere If noise is a dealbreaker, look at printers with linear rail systems or enclosed designs with active dampening If you need the fastest possible prints and don’t mind paying more, the Bambu Lab P1S is faster If you need a large build volume, the Centauri Carbon’s bed is adequate but not huge Bottom Line 6 months in, I’d buy it again. The print quality is the reason. Everything else (speed, noise, software) ranges from good to acceptable. But the prints themselves look great, and that’s why I bought a printer in the first place.
I bought this printer with my own money. This review is not sponsored. Links below are affiliate links, which means I earn a small commission if you buy through them at no extra cost to you.

content:
The Centauri Carbon prints well out of the box, but “well” and “dialed in” are different things. After six months of near-daily printing across eight-plus filament types, these are the OrcaSlicer settings that actually hold up — print to print, not just on the one calibration cube that looks good on YouTube.
This isn’t a copy of someone’s profile export. Every number here came from a tuning pass and a pile of failed parts.
Some links below are affiliate links — if you buy through them I may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. I only point to gear I'd actually use.
Before You Touch Per-Filament Settings Two things matter more than any single slider:
Run a flow-rate (extrusion multiplier) calibration per filament. OrcaSlicer’s built-in calibration tools do this in two prints. Skip it and every other setting fights against bad flow. Calibrate pressure advance. On a bowden-free direct-drive machine like the Centauri, this is what kills the blobs at corners and the bulge after every travel move. Do those two for each new spool brand and most “the printer is bad” problems disappear.
PLA / PLA+ The easy one. The Centauri is nearly flawless here.
Layer height: 0.2mm for daily parts, 0.12mm when the surface shows. Speed: Stock “fast” profile is fine. Rapid PLA+ holds quality at the printer’s recommended fast speeds without visible layer-line degradation. Infill: Gyroid at 15% for functional/daily-use objects — strong enough, fast enough, and it doesn’t telegraph through top surfaces. Overhangs: Clean to ~55° before you need supports. Plan around that and you’ll print supportless more often than you’d expect. PETG (including food-grade and carbon PETG) PETG is where people give up on a machine that’s actually fine. The fix is first-layer discipline.
Slower first layer. This is the single biggest win. PETG wants to be laid down calmly. Higher bed temp than PLA to get adhesion without slamming the nozzle into the plate. Line width: 0.42–0.5mm at 0.2mm layer height worked well for food-grade carbon PETG. Retraction: Keep it modest; over-retracting PETG causes more stringing problems than it solves. Tune pressure advance first, then revisit. Once tuned, PETG is consistent on this machine — it just punishes a lazy first layer.
TPU (flexible) TPU works on the Centauri’s direct drive, but you have to accept it’s slow.
Speed: 30mm/s max. Push past it and you’ll get skips and gaps. Retraction: Disable it. Flexible filament + retraction = jams and inconsistent walls. Patience: Results are genuinely good. Impatient people will hate the print times. There’s no shortcut here; flexibles are slow on every consumer machine. ABS Printable, but it needs ambient heat management — the Centauri isn’t a sealed chamber by default.
Enclose it. I print ABS with the door shut in an enclosed space. Ambient temperature control is the whole game with ABS warping. Bed adhesion: Higher bed temp and a brim. ABS lifts corners the moment it cools unevenly. Drafts are the enemy. A cold breeze across a tall ABS print will split layers. Keep it closed up. If you can’t manage ambient temp, print ASA or a tough PETG instead and save yourself the warping headaches.
PLA-CF (carbon-fiber filled) Use a hardened steel nozzle . Carbon-fiber and glass-filled filaments chew through brass. This is non-negotiable if you want the nozzle to survive. Layer height: 0.2mm. CF filaments don’t reward going ultra-fine; the fibers matter more than the layer lines. Dry the filament. CF blends pick up moisture fast and print rough/popping when wet. A filament dryer pays for itself here. The One Setting Most People Get Wrong First-layer speed. Across every filament above, slowing the first layer fixed more failures than any other change. The Centauri handles slow first layers cleanly, which means fewer failed prints and far less wasted filament over a month of printing. It’s the least glamorous setting and the most important one.
Bottom Line The Centauri Carbon doesn’t need exotic settings — it needs per-filament settings and two calibrations (flow + pressure advance) done honestly. Do that once per spool brand and you’ll spend your time printing instead of troubleshooting.

There are dozens of 3D printing filaments, but 95% of what you print should be one of three: PLA, PETG, or ABS. Pick the wrong one and you get warped parts, failed prints, or objects that melt in a hot car. Here’s how to choose without wasting spools learning the hard way.
Some links below are affiliate links — if you buy through them I may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. I only point to gear I'd actually use.
The 10-Second Answer PLA — your default. Easy to print, cheap, looks great. Use it unless you have a specific reason not to. PETG — when the part needs to survive heat, moisture, or impact. Outdoor and functional parts. ABS — when you need real toughness and high heat resistance, and you have an enclosure. If you’re new: start with PLA. Don’t overthink it. You can learn the others later.
PLA — The Default PLA (polylactic acid) is the easiest filament to print and the reason most people succeed on their first try. Low printing temperature, minimal warping, no enclosure needed.
Use PLA for:
Decorative objects, models, miniatures Prototypes and test prints Indoor functional parts that won’t see heat Anything where appearance matters (it has the best surface finish) Avoid PLA for:
Anything left in a hot car (it softens around 60°C — a sunny dashboard will deform it) Outdoor parts exposed to sun High-stress mechanical parts (it’s stiff but brittle) Cost: Cheapest tier. ~$15-25 per 1kg spool.
Print difficulty: Easiest. Works at stock settings on nearly every printer.
Browse PLA filament on Amazon → PETG — The Practical Workhorse PETG (polyethylene terephthalate glycol) is the “I need this to actually work” filament. It’s tougher than PLA, handles heat and moisture far better, and is more impact-resistant. The tradeoff is it’s slightly fussier to print — stringing is the main annoyance.
Use PETG for:
Functional parts that flex without snapping Outdoor items (planters, brackets, mounts) Anything exposed to water or moderate heat Food-adjacent items (use food-grade PETG and your own judgment) Avoid PETG for:
Highly detailed miniatures (stringing hurts fine detail) Situations where you want a perfect glossy finish without tuning The tuning gotcha: PETG needs a slower first layer, a higher bed temperature, and retraction tuning to control stringing. Budget one calibration pass before you trust it.
Cost: Slightly more than PLA. ~$20-30 per 1kg spool.
Print difficulty: Moderate. Worth the small learning curve.
Browse PETG filament on Amazon → ABS — The Tough One (With Conditions) ABS (acrylonitrile butadiene styrene) is what Lego is made of. It’s tough, machinable, and handles high heat. It’s also the hardest of the three to print well, because it warps badly without a controlled environment.
Use ABS for:
Automotive parts (it survives a hot car where PLA dies) Enclosures and housings that need durability Parts you’ll drill, tap, or post-process with acetone smoothing Avoid ABS if:
You don’t have an enclosure. ABS warps and cracks in open air and drafts. You print in a poorly ventilated room — ABS fumes are unpleasant and you want airflow management. The hard requirement: An enclosure (even a DIY closet or box) and ambient temperature control. Without it, large ABS prints will lift off the bed and crack. This is non-negotiable.
Cost: Similar to PETG. ~$20-30 per 1kg spool.
Print difficulty: Hardest of the three. Don’t start here.
Browse ABS filament on Amazon → Side-by-Side PLA PETG ABS Ease of printing Easiest Moderate Hardest Heat resistance Low (~60°C) Medium (~80°C) High (~100°C) Strength Stiff, brittle Tough, flexible Tough, impact-resistant Enclosure needed No No Yes Surface finish Best Good Good (great with acetone smoothing) Outdoor/UV Poor Good Fair Cost (1kg) $15-25 $20-30 $20-30 Best for Looks, prototypes, indoor Functional, outdoor, moisture Heat, toughness, automotive The Mistakes That Waste Money Buying ABS as a beginner. It will warp, you’ll get frustrated, and you’ll blame the printer. Start with PLA. Using PLA for a car phone mount. It will deform on the first sunny day. Use PETG or ABS. Ignoring filament storage. PETG and especially nylon absorb moisture from the air, which causes popping and poor layer adhesion. A cheap sealed bin with desiccant solves it. Not doing a tuning pass per material. Each filament wants different temps and retraction. The “one profile for everything” approach produces mediocre prints across the board. What to Buy First If you own a printer and need a starting kit:
2 spools of PLA in colors you like — this covers most of what you’ll print early on. 1 spool of PETG for when you make something that needs to survive the real world. Skip ABS until you have an enclosure and a specific need. Bottom Line PLA for looks and ease. PETG for function and the outdoors. ABS for heat and toughness when you have an enclosure. Most people never need anything else — and the ones who do already know it.
Filament prices fluctuate. We keep this guide current as the market shifts.

You print miniatures, tabletop terrain, or small functional parts. Desk space is tight (dorm, apartment, shared room). You want the lowest entry price into Bambu. content:
Half the “my printer is broken” problems I’ve chased turned out to be wet filament. It mimics real hardware faults — popping sounds, stringing, rough surfaces, weak parts — so people tear down a perfectly good machine when the fix was a few hours in a dryer.
Here’s how to tell, and what to do.
Some links below are affiliate links — if you buy through them I may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. I only point to gear I'd actually use.
Signs Your Filament Is Wet Wet filament gives itself away. Watch and listen for:
Popping or crackling from the nozzle while printing — that’s trapped moisture flashing to steam. Stringing and oozing that no retraction tuning fixes. If you’ve dialed retraction and it still strings, suspect moisture. Rough, fuzzy, or inconsistent surfaces where it used to print smooth. Weak, brittle parts that snap along layer lines — steam disrupts layer bonding. Visible steam or a “fizzy” extrusion in bad cases. The tell is when a filament that used to print fine suddenly prints badly. The spool didn’t change — its moisture content did.
Which Filaments Absorb Water Fastest Not all filament is equally thirsty. Roughly worst to best:
Nylon / PA — drinks water out of the air. Almost always needs drying. PLA-CF and other carbon/glass-filled blends — the fibers wick moisture fast. Mine prints rough and popping within days of being left out. TPU — flexible filaments are moisture-sensitive. PETG — moderate; noticeable when humid. PLA — most forgiving, but still degrades over months in a humid room. If you live somewhere humid, even PLA benefits from storage discipline.
How to Dry Filament Two realistic options:
A dedicated filament dryer (best). A filament dryer box holds a set temperature and many let you print straight from the box. This is the set-and-forget answer and what I use for CF blends.
PLA: ~45-50°C for 4-6 hours PETG: ~55-65°C for 4-6 hours TPU: ~50°C for 4-6 hours PLA-CF / Nylon: ~70°C for 6-8+ hours Your oven (works in a pinch, with caution). Lowest setting, ideally with an oven thermometer because home ovens overshoot. Stay near the glass-transition temp — too hot and the spool fuses into a useless brick. Honestly, a dryer is cheaper than the filament you’ll ruin learning your oven’s true temperature.
How to Keep It Dry Drying is treating the symptom. Storage is the cure:
Airtight container + desiccant between prints. Cheap and effective. Print from a dry box for the thirsty filaments (CF, nylon, TPU). Don’t leave spools on the printer for weeks. That’s how “it printed fine last month” becomes today’s failed print. Bottom Line Before you blame the printer, blame the spool. Wet filament is the most common invisible cause of bad prints, and it’s the easiest to fix. Dry it, store it sealed with desiccant, and a whole category of “printer problems” disappears.
For the broader failure checklist, see why your 3D print is failing. For per-filament print settings, see the PLA vs PETG vs ABS guide.
summary:
Half the “my printer is broken” problems I’ve chased turned out to be wet filament. It mimics real hardware faults — popping sounds, stringing, rough surfaces, weak parts — so people tear down a perfectly good machine when the fix was a few hours in a dryer.

Here’s how to tell, and what to do.

Every 3D print failure has a cause, and almost all of them fall into one of a dozen buckets. This is the troubleshooting checklist worth bookmarking — symptoms, causes, and the fixes that actually work, in rough order of how often they bite people.
Some links below are affiliate links — if you buy through them I may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. I only point to gear I'd actually use.
1. First Layer Won’t Stick The single most common failure. If the first layer doesn’t adhere, nothing else matters.
Fixes, in order:
Re-level the bed (or re-run auto bed leveling). 80% of adhesion problems are leveling. Lower the nozzle slightly — adjust your Z-offset down in small steps (0.02-0.05mm). Clean the bed. Fingerprint oils kill adhesion. Wipe with isopropyl alcohol. Raise bed temperature 5°C. For PLA try 60°C, PETG 75-80°C. Slow the first layer to ~20mm/s. Add a brim in your slicer for extra surface contact. 2. Warping (Corners Lifting) The print curls up at the edges, especially with ABS and large flat parts.
Fixes:
Use a brim or raft for more bed grip. Eliminate drafts — an enclosure makes the biggest difference for ABS. Raise bed temp and keep the chamber warm. Switch material — if you don’t have an enclosure, PETG or PLA warps far less than ABS. 3. Stringing (Wispy Threads Between Parts) Thin strands of filament strung across gaps, most common with PETG.
Fixes:
Increase retraction distance and speed in your slicer. Lower print temperature 5-10°C — too hot causes oozing. Enable “wipe” and “combing” in your slicer. Dry your filament — moisture is a major stringing cause (especially PETG and nylon). 4. Layer Shifting (Print Suddenly Offset) Upper layers misalign with lower ones, ruining the print mid-way.
Fixes:
Reduce print speed and acceleration — shifts often come from the toolhead moving faster than the motors can keep up. Check belt tension — loose belts skip steps. Make sure nothing’s obstructing the gantry — a stray clip or cable can cause a skip. 5. Under-Extrusion (Gaps, Thin Layers) Not enough plastic coming out — weak, gappy prints.
Fixes:
Check for a partial clog — do a cold pull or run cleaning filament. Increase flow rate / extrusion multiplier slightly. Raise temperature 5°C so plastic flows more easily. Inspect the extruder gear for ground-down filament (a sign of a jam upstream). 6. Over-Extrusion (Blobs, Rough Top) Too much plastic — messy surfaces and dimensional inaccuracy.
Fixes:
Lower flow rate / extrusion multiplier. Calibrate your E-steps (extruder steps) if it’s persistent. Reduce temperature slightly. 7. Clogged Nozzle Nothing extrudes, or extrusion stops mid-print.
Fixes:
Cold pull — heat, then pull filament out to remove the clog. Use a cleaning needle to clear the nozzle. Replace the nozzle — they’re cheap and wear out, especially with abrasive filaments like PLA-CF. 8. Poor Overhangs / Drooping Steep angles sag or fail.
Fixes:
Improve cooling — turn up the part cooling fan for PLA. Add supports for overhangs beyond ~50-55°. Slow down on overhang regions. Orient the part to minimize steep overhangs in the first place. 9. Elephant’s Foot (Bulging First Layers) The bottom layers bulge outward.
Fixes:
Lower bed temperature slightly. Raise the Z-offset a touch. Enable “elephant foot compensation” in your slicer. 10. Ghosting / Ringing (Echoes Near Edges) Faint ripples after sharp corners.
Fixes:
Lower acceleration and jerk. Tighten belts. Make sure the printer sits on a solid, stable surface — a wobbly table amplifies it. 11. Spaghetti (Print Detaches and Becomes a Mess) The print comes loose and the nozzle keeps extruding into air.
Fixes:
Almost always a first-layer adhesion failure (see #1) — fix that first. Add a brim, clean the bed, re-level. On printers with failure detection, enable it so you don’t waste a whole spool. 12. Wet Filament (Popping, Rough Surface, Weak Layers) Filament that’s absorbed moisture from the air.
Fixes:
Dry it — a filament dryer, or a few hours in an oven at low temp (check your filament’s safe temp). Store filament sealed with desiccant going forward. PETG, TPU, and nylon are the worst offenders; PLA is more forgiving. The Universal First Three Checks When a print fails and you don’t know why, check these before anything else:
Is the bed level and clean? Is the filament dry? Are you printing too fast for the part? Those three account for the large majority of failures. Master them and your success rate jumps dramatically.
Tools Worth Having A filament dryer — fixes a whole category of problems. A spare nozzle set — clogs happen; swapping is faster than clearing. Isopropyl alcohol + a glue stick — the cheapest adhesion insurance there is. Got a failure not on this list? The cause is almost always temperature, adhesion, speed, or moisture. Work through those four and you’ll find it.

PETG is a great filament that scares people off because of the first layer. It either won’t stick at all, or it sticks too well and tears chunks out of your bed. Both come down to a handful of settings. Here are the fixes in the order I’d actually try them.
Some links below are affiliate links — if you buy through them I may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. I only point to gear I'd actually use.
First, the Counterintuitive Part PETG’s problem usually isn’t too little adhesion — it’s inconsistent adhesion from a first layer that’s rushed or squished wrong. Fix the first layer and most “PETG won’t stick” complaints vanish. Work down this list in order; stop when it sticks.
1. Slow the First Layer Down This is the single biggest fix. PETG wants to be laid down calmly — try a first-layer speed around 20-25 mm/s. A rushed first layer is the #1 cause of poor PETG adhesion. If you change one thing, change this.
2. Raise the Bed Temperature PETG likes a warmer bed than PLA. Start around 75-80°C and adjust. Too cool and the first layer never grabs; the right temp lets it settle and bond.
3. Get the Z-Offset Right PETG is fussier about first-layer height than PLA. You want the lines slightly squished into the plate — not floating (won’t stick) and not so crushed the nozzle drags (causes the opposite problem). Re-run a Z-offset calibration specifically for PETG; the value that’s perfect for PLA is often a touch too high for PETG.
4. Clean the Bed (Really Clean It) Finger oils kill adhesion. Wash the plate with warm water and dish soap, or wipe with isopropyl alcohol. Do this more often than you think — a bed that worked yesterday can fail today from one handprint.
5. Match the Surface to PETG Textured PEI: great for PETG — strong but releases cleanly once cool. Smooth PEI: PETG can bond too hard and tear the sheet. Use a release agent here (a thin glue-stick layer doubles as a barrier so PETG doesn’t weld to the plate). Glass: needs glue stick or hairspray as a barrier. The glue stick on smooth surfaces isn’t for more grip — it’s a barrier so PETG doesn’t fuse to the bed and rip it.
6. Kill Drafts and Cooling PETG hates aggressive part cooling on the first layers. Drop the cooling fan to 0-30% for the first few layers, and keep cold air off the bed. A draft across the plate causes uneven cooling and corner lifting.
7. Check If the Filament Is Wet If you’ve done all the above and still get poor, bubbly, or popping first layers, the filament may be wet — PETG absorbs moisture and prints rough when it does. See how to dry filament to rule it out.
The Order That Usually Works For most people the fix is: slow first layer + correct bed temp + clean bed + dialed Z-offset. That combination solves the large majority of PETG adhesion problems. Add a release barrier if you’re on smooth PEI or glass, and manage cooling/drafts for tall prints.
Bottom Line PETG isn’t hard — it’s just less forgiving than PLA on the first layer. Slow it down, warm the bed, clean the surface, and dial the Z-offset. Once it’s tuned it’s one of the most useful filaments you can run.

The best first 3D printer is the one that doesn’t make you quit. Most people who give up on 3D printing don’t quit because it’s hard — they quit because they bought a machine that needed constant tuning and spent their first weekend fighting it instead of making things. Here’s how to skip that.
Some links below are affiliate links — if you buy through them I may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. I only point to gear I'd actually use.
The One-Line Answer Get a Bambu Lab A1 (or A1 Mini if space is tight). It’s the closest thing to a printer that “just works” at a beginner-friendly price, and that matters more than any spec when you’re starting out.
If print quality matters more to you than convenience and you don’t mind a little tuning, the Elegoo Centauri Carbon is the alternative — we reviewed it after 6 months of daily use.
Why “Easy” Beats “Powerful” for Your First Printer A more capable printer that requires expertise is worse for a beginner than a simpler one that works reliably. You can’t appreciate advanced features until you’ve mastered the basics, and you can’t master the basics if every print is a coin flip.
The machines that make beginners successful share three traits:
Automatic bed leveling — removes the #1 source of beginner failures. Tested slicer profiles — so you don’t have to guess temperatures and speeds. Reliable first layers — the foundation of every print. The Bambu A1 nails all three. That’s why it’s the default recommendation.
What to Avoid as a Beginner Cheap kit printers that require full assembly. Building it yourself sounds educational, but it front-loads frustration before you’ve made a single thing. Resin printers as a first machine. Incredible detail, but messy, smelly, and they involve handling chemicals. Start with filament (FDM), add resin later if you get into miniatures. ABS as a first filament. It warps without an enclosure and will make you think you broke the printer. Start with PLA. The absolute cheapest printer you can find. The $50-100 you save often costs you the hobby entirely when the machine frustrates you out of it. Your Realistic First-Purchase Budget Printer: $200-350 (Bambu A1 Mini to A1) Filament: $30-50 for two or three spools of PLA to start Basic tools: ~$20 (most printers include a starter set; a deburring tool and good flush cutters help) Optional: a dry box if you’re somewhere humid Total to actually start making things: ~$300-400.
Check the Bambu Lab A1 price on Amazon → Check the Bambu Lab A1 Mini price on Amazon → The First-Week Plan (So You Don’t Quit) Print the test model that ships with the printer first. Don’t change anything. Confirm the machine works out of the box. Print a Benchy (the classic boat torture test). It reveals stringing, overhang, and bridging issues at a glance. Print something you actually want. A phone stand, a desk organizer, a small toy. Early motivation comes from making something useful. Only then start tuning. Once you’ve had a few successes, learn to dial in settings for different filaments. Where to Get Models to Print You don’t need to design anything to start. Free model sites have millions of ready-to-print files:
Printables and MakerWorld — huge libraries, beginner-friendly, free. Thingiverse — the original, still massive. Start with “print-in-place” models (things that print fully assembled, no support needed) — they’re satisfying and forgiving.
What You’ll Want Next (But Don’t Need Yet) Once you’re hooked, the natural upgrades are:
A second filament type (PETG, for functional/outdoor parts — see our filament guide) A filament dryer (fixes a whole category of quality issues) An enclosure (if you move into ABS) Multi-color (Bambu’s AMS system) None of this is necessary on day one. Buy the printer, buy PLA, make things.
Bottom Line Your first 3D printer should remove obstacles, not add them. The Bambu Lab A1 is the safest bet for most beginners in 2026 — it works out of the box, and “it works” is the only feature that matters when you’re learning. Spend your energy making things, not tuning a machine.

Most 3D printing questions have a frustrating answer: it depends. Enclosures are no different. Whether you need one comes down to what material you’re printing, where your printer lives, and how many failed prints you’re willing to tolerate. Here’s the honest breakdown.
Some links below are affiliate links — if you buy through them I may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. I only point to gear I'd actually use.
What an Enclosure Actually Does A 3d printer enclosure does two things: traps heat and blocks drafts. That sounds simple, but both matter more than most people realize.
Drafts kill tall prints. A ceiling fan, an HVAC vent, someone walking past the room — any airflow can cause uneven cooling that splits layer bonds or warps corners off the bed. An enclosure eliminates that variable entirely.
Trapped heat lets you print materials that need a warm ambient temperature to stay stable. ABS wants roughly 40–50°C chamber temperature. Without it, you’ll fight warping and layer delamination regardless of how dialed-in your other settings are.
When You Actually Need One If you’re printing ABS, ASA, or nylon, an enclosure isn’t optional — it’s required. These materials shrink as they cool. Too fast, and corners lift. Too much temperature differential, and the whole print cracks down the middle. Good ABS filament is wasted effort if your chamber is open to room air.
If your printer is in a drafty or cold space, an enclosure will improve print quality across all materials — even PLA and PETG don’t need one technically, but tall thin prints in a drafty garage will thank you for it.
If you care about fumes and particles, a sealed enclosure with a HEPA/carbon filter is worth it. All FDM printing releases ultrafine particles. ABS and ASA release more, including styrene. If your printer is in a bedroom or shared living space, that’s not trivial.
When You Don’t Need One PLA on a well-tuned printer in a normal room doesn’t need an enclosure. Most hobbyist printing is PLA. If you’re making functional parts, miniatures, or prototypes in PLA, an enclosure adds no print quality benefit — it can actually cause problems by trapping heat and causing heat creep on hotends not designed for it.
PETG is mostly the same story. It’s more tolerant of temperature swings than ABS and doesn’t warp badly at room temperature. An enclosure is optional at best for PETG. See PLA vs PETG vs ABS for the full breakdown on which material actually needs what.
If your printer already has one built in, like any of the Bambu enclosed models, this question is already answered for you.
What They Cost DIY options — an Ikea Lack table stack, a cardboard box with foil tape on the gaps — can run under $30 and work reasonably well for ABS if you seal properly. Not pretty, but functional.
Purpose-built enclosures start around $80–120 for basic panel designs. A proper 3D printer enclosure with magnetic panels, a viewing window, and ventilation ports makes a real difference in usability — you can run it with an inline filter and route fumes outside if needed.
At the high end, enclosed printers like the Bambu X1 Carbon build the chamber into the machine. If you’re buying new hardware and planning to print engineering filaments regularly, that’s worth considering over a bare printer plus an aftermarket enclosure bolted on.
One thing enclosures don’t fix: bad bed adhesion, wet filament, under-extrusion, or a miscalibrated first layer. If your prints are already failing, check why your 3D print is failing before buying any hardware.
Does the Material Matter? Less than people think. The only goal is trapping heat and blocking drafts. Cardboard works. Acrylic works. Metal works. What matters is how well it seals, not what it’s made of.
Avoid anything that fully blocks your sightlines — you want to see the first few layers. And if you’re running ABS or ASA regularly, add a carbon filter. The fumes aren’t theoretical.
Bottom Line You need a 3d printer enclosure if you’re printing ABS, ASA, or nylon — full stop. You almost certainly don’t need one for PLA. PETG falls in the middle and usually does fine without one.
If your printer lives somewhere drafty or cold, an enclosure helps regardless of material. If it’s in a bedroom or occupied room, enclosure plus filter is worth it for air quality alone, no matter what you’re printing.
